1.0.0.en: Nehemiah: a Hebrew name meaning "God has comforted."

1.0.1.en: Chislev: corresponds to the month of December.

1.0.2.en: The twentieth year: the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, king of the kingdom of Media and Persia, which ruled the world at that time.

1.0.3.en: Shushan the palace: the capital of Media and Persia, located in the south-west of Persia, that is, present-day Iran, 200 miles east of Babylon.

1.0.4.en: Nehemiah, the writer of this book, specifies the place and time of the events that follow in this chapter: while Nehemiah was in the city of Shushan the palace, in the month of Chislev, what is told in the following verses took place.

1.1.0.en: The Jews: the people of God used to be called the Hebrews, after Abraham who crossed the river Euphrates and lived in Canaan. But after the captivity the people were called Jews, after the tribe of Judah, which represented the southern kingdom that was taken captive after the northern kingdom. When the people of God returned, they returned as one undivided kingdom, and all of them were called Jews.

1.1.1.en: Nehemiah's concern for his people and his city Jerusalem is evident: his position in the royal palace did not distract him from caring about the news of those who dwelt in Jerusalem. Perhaps he went out of the palace at this time and met one of his relatives according to the flesh, named Hanani, and he calls him "my brother" because he was of the same tribe, the tribe of Levi. Hanani and some of the Jews were returning from a journey to Jerusalem, where they had visited their homeland and their relatives, so Nehemiah asked them about the Jews living in Jerusalem who had escaped death during the Babylonian attack in which the inhabitants of Jerusalem were taken captive.

1.1.2.en: May you care for your relatives and loved ones, especially the weak, for they are the ones in need, so that you ask about their news and try to help them. Do not let the concerns of life and your own needs distract you from your needy brethren.

1.2.0.en: Nehemiah heard bad news about the Jews who remained in Jerusalem: that they were in weakness and misery, because the walls of Jerusalem were still broken down since the Babylonian attack and its great gates were burned with fire. That is, the city was without protection and the people living in it were exposed to attack by any enemy. They were also in shame and disgrace, because all the surrounding cities and neighboring lands were fortified with strong walls and gates, as was the custom of that time; that is, Jerusalem had become a despised and humiliated city, and this had lasted for 140 years since the days of the Babylonian attack.

1.3.0.en: When Nehemiah heard the news of the ruined Jerusalem, he entered his chamber and sat quietly before God. He felt sorrow, not over Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of the walls and the city, because this had been known for a long time, but he was grieved, and even wept, over his sense of his own failure and the failure of all the Jews toward their God and His holy city Jerusalem, in which stood the temple of God, the holiest place in the world. Perhaps he asked himself, how can I live in a great palace while the holy city's walls are broken down?

1.3.1.en: He found nothing before him but to take refuge in God in fasting, declaring his readiness to strip himself of all the material things he enjoyed for God's sake. He came forward to pray in contrition and supplication to God, that He might help him and help all who love God and believe in Him, so that they might care for His holy city Jerusalem.

1.3.2.en: Nehemiah continued in his seclusion, fasting, prayers and tears for days. This was not a passing emotion but deep feelings asking God for help, so that they might be turned into strong works that please Him. The number of days he spent in seclusion is not mentioned, but it is clear that it was not a short period, spent in private seclusion with God away from the eyes of people, because his hope was firm in God, who alone is able to do all things.

1.4.0.en: The God of heaven: an expression for God used after the Babylonian captivity, which destroyed the temple, because this expression proclaims God's dwelling place, which cannot be destroyed, namely heaven.

1.4.1.en: Nehemiah began his prayer, which continues to the end of this chapter, declaring in reverence that he stood before the great God, the God of heaven, to distinguish Him from the pagan gods on earth, and because God is the only God and is feared by all His creation for His greatness and majesty.

1.4.2.en: At the same time He is a compassionate God who cares for His children who believe in Him, who keep His commandments and hold fast to His covenants. He never forsakes them but shepherds them and upholds them if they take refuge in Him. So Nehemiah here seeks God's mercies, that He may have compassion on him and on all his brethren the Jews, His people who worship Him and need His help to build His holy city.

1.5.0.en: In humility he raised his voice before God, feeling his unworthiness because of the multitude of his sins. As one responsible for his people, he came before God on their behalf, bearing their sins and entreating Him, confessing the neglect of building the holy city, although he had not been with them, and those who had fallen short were the Jews living in Jerusalem; but as a true servant he offered repentance for all his people. And because he was unworthy, he entreated God to allow Him to open His ear to hear his prayer and to look with His eyes upon the humiliation of his people. For though they were unworthy, they were His needy children, and he was confident of His fatherhood, which never forsakes them. He borrows the ear and the eye and ascribes them to God, to express the extent of his faith in the God who was before him and his great need of His intervention.

1.5.1.en: Nehemiah was not charged with the responsibility of building Jerusalem, but out of his love for God and for His city he felt responsible. Perhaps he realized at that time that God might have permitted him this great position in the royal palace so that he might serve God and build His city. He kept repeating these words in different phrases and expressions throughout the days of his seclusion, insistently asking for God's intervention. Indeed, the day was not enough for him to pray, but he spent a long part of the night in vigil, with supplications and tears, that God might have mercy on him and on all his people.

1.5.2.en: Nehemiah is an example of the spiritual man whose heart is attached to God more than to all the material things around him, who feels for his brethren before himself, and for the glory of God before any personal benefit, so that he had these deep feelings while far from Jerusalem, whereas most of those who lived in Jerusalem felt nothing of these feelings.

1.6.0.en: We have dealt corruptly: we committed sins that corrupted our life and separated us from God.

1.6.1.en: Nehemiah remembered the sins of his people over tens of years, which led to God's discipline of them by captivity and the burning of the temple. So today he comes forward declaring that the cause of the broken walls and the burned gates is their sins. He speaks in the first person plural, declaring his responsibility for all the evils his people did, and for the failures in worshiping God and keeping His commandments, which they received at the hand of Moses the prophet.

1.7.0.en: He reminds God of His promises in His Law (Deut 30:1-5): that if His people forsook His commandments and worshiped idols, that is, betrayed God, He would scatter them and disperse them among the peoples, and this indeed happened in the captivity. But he completes his words by reminding God of His promises that if they repented and returned to Him, He would gather them from their dispersion, even if they were in all parts of the world, and bring them back to their land to worship Him in His holy temple in Jerusalem, where God chose this place for His dwelling.

1.7.1.en: When he says "remember," this does not mean that God has forgotten, but Nehemiah declares his faith in God's Law and holds Him to His promises, and this rejoices God's heart.

1.8.0.en: He reminds God that the Jews are His people whom He chose from among all peoples because they believed in Him and worshiped Him, and that He saved them and redeemed them from the hands of the Egyptians by the slaying of the Passover lamb, by whose blood He saved their firstborn from death, delivered them and brought them out of Egypt, and parted the Red Sea before them and brought them across, at the time when the firstborn of Egypt were killed and Pharaoh and all his army were drowned. And this is, of course, a type of Christ, the Redeemer of mankind.

1.9.0.en: At the end of the prayer he repeated his petition that God would hear his prayer and even give him favor before the king whom Nehemiah served, for he was working as cupbearer to the king, which is a high position with a large number of workers under it. For, by God's guidance, many ideas came to his mind by which he could build the broken walls, and they needed the king's approval, and he was confident that God was able to persuade the king to agree to all his requests, so that he would succeed in building the walls.

1.9.1.en: And in faith Nehemiah trusted that there were believing Jews, whether in Jerusalem, or with him in Shushan the palace, or throughout the kingdom, who cared about Jerusalem and were praying to God for its rebuilding and the building of its walls. Perhaps this feeling reached him not only from his brethren the Jews who told him about Jerusalem, but he sensed by God's guidance that there were others who lifted up prayer before God, and this shows the extent of Nehemiah's faith, for he did not despair and did not feel that he was alone, as Elijah felt long ago (1 Kgs 18:22). Nehemiah held the position of the king's cupbearer, and whether he was the chief of the cupbearers or one of the senior cupbearers who stood before the king, it is a position of special standing, because he was near the king at all times, whether during his work or his rest, whenever he needed to drink. This allowed a very close personal relationship and friendship with the king. He was entrusted with the king's life, since he would pour drops of the drink, whether wine or another, into the palm of his left hand and taste them before the king, to assure the king that the drink was free of poison, thereby declaring his readiness to redeem the king's life from any harm. The position of Nehemiah was already discussed in the introduction to this book. And we see in this prayer Nehemiah's faith, which appeared in his calling on God to intervene, as follows:

1.9.2.en: 1- Reminding Him of what He said in His Law and of His promise to gather His scattered people if they repented and returned to Him.

1.9.3.en: 2- That God is able to build these walls, just as He rescued His people long ago from the bondage of Egypt and redeemed them.

1.9.4.en: 3- That the people of God are His servants, who keep His commandments and love Him, that is, they are His own, whom He must intervene to support.

1.9.5.en: 4- That His people want to live in His fear, for they strive spiritually to please Him, and He never forsakes those who draw near to Him, even if they are weak and fall short, so long as they want to please Him. He helps them to worship Him faithfully and builds the holy city for them, so that they may be at ease and practice their worship in all freedom in His holy temple.

1.9.6.en: God greatly rejoices when you draw near to Him and in your earnest prayer toward Him. So place your problems before God every day and be insistent with Him, and do not leave Him, confident that He rejoices in your prayers and never forsakes you, and that He works miracles to bring about your good, so that you live with Him forever.

1.9.7.en: The king sends Nehemiah to build the walls

2.0.s.en: (1) The king's approval of Nehemiah's requests

2.0.0.en: The month of Nisan: corresponds to the month of April.

2.0.1.en: The twentieth year: the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes. Its beginning is not tied to the beginning of the civil year but starts in one of its months. Four months passed between the months of Chislev and Nisan (December and April), from Nehemiah's hearing the news of the ruined Jerusalem to his coming before the king mentioned in this chapter.

2.0.2.en: Sad (of countenance): a manifestation of deep grief on the face.

2.0.3.en: A large number of cupbearers worked for the king, each with his own turn. Every few or several months the cupbearer's turn comes to take care of serving drinks to the king. Four months passed between the events of the first chapter and this chapter, and this shows that the days Nehemiah spent in his seclusion, which are referred to simply as days, took a period that was not short, which may have extended to a month or two in retreat. When Nehemiah's turn came to serve wine and drinks to the king, four months had passed since he had heard the news of the broken walls and the burned gates, and the sorrow of his heart was so deep that it showed on his face throughout this period, and he could not hide it when he came before the king, although it was dangerous for the cupbearer to appear with sorrow on his face, lest the king be angry, especially since Nehemiah was a spiritual man who believed in God, so the cheerfulness of his face was clear and expressed his deep joy, and therefore a great difference showed when his face was sad.

2.1.0.en: When the king noticed the signs of sorrow on Nehemiah's face, he asked him the reason for his sorrow although he was not sick, because sickness sometimes causes pains that make the face sad. Then the king continued, saying that these signs of sorrow show that your heart is sad. So Nehemiah was afraid, because it was customary at that time for the king's personal attendants to appear before him with joy and a smile, and if they appeared otherwise they were liable to be put to death.

2.2.0.en: Nehemiah answered the king with the greeting and honor customary at that time, praying that he might live forever. Then he told him the reason for the sadness of his face, which was his discovery that the city of his fathers, in which their tombs are located, was in ruins, without walls, and that its gates were burned. The ancients prized the tombs of their fathers, and it grieved them that these should not be under protection inside fortified cities, and that any tampering with these tombs insulted them and distressed them greatly. By this Nehemiah aroused the king's sympathy with him and made him feel his problem and sorrows. He did not say to the king that he wanted to build Jerusalem and fortify it, so that the king would not fear the building of fortified cities that might rebel against him one day, but said that it was merely the city of his fathers' tombs, so that he would sympathize with him.

2.3.0.en: Here appears God's grace in the king's response to Nehemiah and his readiness to meet his requests to solve his problem, and he even asked him to specify his requests. Here Nehemiah appears as a spiritual man: he lifted his heart in prayer that God might give him wisdom in the eyes of the king and guide him to the requests he should make. Despite his deep prayers and fasts throughout four months, he now prays again in the king's presence that God may speak through his tongue, for the cupbearers were not permitted to ask anything of the king by exploiting their position and their nearness to him. But through prayer Nehemiah believed that God was able to give him favor in the eyes of the king, so that he would grant his requests and not be angry with him.

2.3.1.en: How beautiful it is that you take refuge in God at all times and in all situations, that He may support you and you experience His power, and on the other hand that you enjoy speaking with God throughout the day and feel the beauty of fellowship with Him.

2.4.0.en: With courtesy and humility Nehemiah said to the king that if he was pleased with him and felt that his requests were suitable, he would allow him to go to the region of Judah, in which is the land of his fathers and of which Jerusalem is the capital, to build it and repair it because it was in ruins.

2.5.0.en: King Artaxerxes was sitting with the queen beside him, and perhaps the queen had a part in the matter of Nehemiah, that is, she spoke with the king in a side conversation to encourage him to sympathize with Nehemiah. It is possible that this queen was Esther, the wife of King Ahasuerus, the father of Artaxerxes, and so she would be his mother, or like a mother to Artaxerxes.

2.5.1.en: The king agreed to Nehemiah's first request, to allow him to go to Jerusalem to build it, and asked him for the details of his mission, that is, the date of his departure and the length of time he wanted to spend there. By God's guidance Nehemiah specified the period he needed so that the king would grant him this leave from his work as cupbearer. This period was probably months or a year, which he renewed afterward. It is possible that Nehemiah did not stay in Jerusalem the twelve years until it reached him, as is mentioned in this book (ch. 13:6), but he may have returned once or several times to Shushan the palace, and then returned to Jerusalem again.

2.6.0.en: Beyond the river: the lands lying around the river Jordan.

2.6.1.en: Nehemiah presented his second request to the king, which was to obtain letters from the king to the governors under his authority in the region surrounding the Jordan to the east and west, so that they would allow him to pass through their lands until he reached Judah.

2.7.0.en: The king's forest: the king's gardens with their many trees.

2.7.1.en: The palace which appertained to the house: a building beside the house, which is the temple of God.

2.7.2.en: The house that I shall enter into: the dwelling of Nehemiah, who was responsible on behalf of the king for the building of Jerusalem.

2.7.3.en: After Nehemiah asked the king for leave to travel to Jerusalem (v. 6) and then asked permission to pass through the lands beyond the Jordan (v. 7), he made his third request in this verse, which was for a letter to the keeper of the king's gardens, which are in the region of Jerusalem, so that he might take timber from them to build the palace attached to the temple of God, in which are storerooms and annexes for the service, as well as timber to build the wall of the city and its gates, and finally timber to build a dwelling for Nehemiah himself. So he cares for the temple of God and the city, and in the end asks for what is necessary for himself, namely a dwelling in which to live. He put the building of the palace before the wall so as to show the king his concern for the worship of God in the city where his fathers lived and where their tombs are, and that his concern was not for Jerusalem to be a great and fortified city, so as not to arouse the king's fears about it. By God's grace the king agreed to all of Nehemiah's requests, and Nehemiah felt that he was receiving his requests from the hand of God through the king, for his direct dealing was with God before people. Most likely the king gave to him generously, as God moved him, because it was the good hand of God that gave to Nehemiah, and He is the One "that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not" (Jas 1:5).

2.8.s.en: (2) Nehemiah in Jerusalem and the displeasure of the enemies

2.8.0.en: God's grace appeared with Nehemiah in the king's concern to send soldiers with him to guard him and the few Jews who accompanied him (v. 11). So Nehemiah moved as an official representative of the king, guarded by a military company, which gave him awe in the eyes of the governors beyond the Jordan, and they received him with welcome, especially when they read the king's letters to them. And so he passed through their lands until he arrived at Jerusalem.

2.8.1.en: God is ready to give you graces from Himself that you did not ask for, and awe in the eyes of those around you. So do not fear the wicked, but use this awe to win everyone for Christ, so that along with their respect for you they see your love and are drawn to your Christ.

2.9.0.en: Sanballat the Horonite: from the city of Horonaim, which lies in the south of Moab and 30 km north-west of Jerusalem. He was a chief and governor in the city of Samaria and hated the Jews, because their strength frightened the Samaritans, so he worked to weaken them.

2.9.1.en: Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite: he was a servant of the king and at the same time chief of the children of Ammon, who lived east of the Dead Sea. This people were descended from Lot and were hostile to the children of Israel.

2.9.2.en: It grieved them: a wrong, any matter that saddens and angers.

2.9.3.en: When the enemies of the children of Israel heard, represented by the leaders of some of the cities and peoples surrounding the people of God, namely Sanballat and Tobiah, they were greatly distressed, because Nehemiah's coming meant good and blessing for Jerusalem and Judah, since whenever Judah was weak these enemies felt their own strength, but if it was strong they feared it.

2.10.s.en: (3) Surveying the city and the walls

2.10.0.en: Nehemiah arrived at Jerusalem and stayed there three days, examining the city and the walls and learning about all that had happened in it. Nehemiah here is a type of Christ, who stayed three days in the tomb and after this rose from the dead, just as Nehemiah arose to build the city.

2.11.0.en: Because of the disgrace in which the ruined Jerusalem lay, Nehemiah set out by night and arose with the small group of Jews who had come with him from Shushan the palace, and they went out on a secret mission to survey the walls and the city. Nehemiah rode on a beast and moved quietly, and he told none of the leaders of Jerusalem about the great work he wished to do, which was building the wall and the city, especially since there were enemies who were concerned that nothing beneficial be done for Jerusalem. Nehemiah was not shaken by their opposition, but he was careful that his mission should be secret, lest he give the enemies an opportunity to increase their opposition.

2.11.1.en: Great works need examination with patience and calm with oneself before taking great decisions. Calm with prayer and fasting makes you obtain God's mercies and guidance easily. So do not rush into any great matter in your life, but give yourself a chance to hear the voice of God.

2.12.0.en: The valley gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, located in its south-west, overlooking the valley of Hinnom adjoining Jerusalem, where the remains of animals and everything left over from the city were thrown and burned with fire, so the fire was always burning in it, and from it the word Gehenna was taken. It is a type of eternal torment, and the valley gate signifies the need for tears and repentance for deliverance from judgment and eternal torment. The dragon well: a statue of a dragon from whose mouth water came out, and this spring was beside the valley gate.

2.12.1.en: The dung gate: dung is the manure of animals, that is, their waste, because in front of this gate the manure of animals was thrown. So this gate signifies the importance of being cleansed from every impurity, to which the manure thrown far from the city through this gate points. From this point Nehemiah tells in detail how he began to examine the walls of the city, and it is evident that his movement was in the southern part of the city wall, which was the remaining part of the wall, because the enemies' attacks mostly came from the north of the city and its east, so of the wall in these directions only a few traces remained. So he moved from the valley gate toward the dung gate, a distance of about 1 km, and went on examining the broken walls and the burned gates. All this was done by night, away from the eyes of the enemies, so that he might arrange his affairs and take his decisions for rebuilding the wall.

2.12.2.en: The mention of these two gates signifies the importance of repentance and purity for beginning the spiritual building.

2.13.0.en: The fountain gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, located east of the dung gate, beside which is a pool in which the water of the spring near the gate was stored. This pool is called the pool of Siloam or the king's pool because it is near the king's garden, that is, his gardens (2 Kgs 25:4, Jer 52:7). Nehemiah continued examining the wall, so he crossed from the dung gate along the wall to the fountain gate, and there the wall had become so broken down and narrow that he found no place for the beast he was riding to pass. We notice that Nehemiah began examining the wall in the southern part, which had not been broken down as much as the wall in the northern part. He is a positive person who sees the sound part of the wall in some measure before the part that was almost completely broken down, in order to strengthen hope in himself and in those with him.

2.14.0.en: After that Nehemiah passed through a valley and went up one of the mountains, because Jerusalem is built on five mountains, and from the mountain he was able to see a considerable part of the wall. Then he returned to where he had begun, that is, to the valley gate.

2.15.0.en: The rulers: the leaders of the city of Jerusalem.

2.15.1.en: The nobles: the great and the rich.

2.15.2.en: Nehemiah examined the wall with a few of the Jews who had come with him from Shushan the palace, and this mission was completely secret. He told neither the rulers, nor the priests, nor the nobles, nor all the people, as a precaution against the enemies, lest they know his plan and increase their opposition.

2.16.0.en: After the secret examination of Jerusalem and its walls, Nehemiah gathered the rulers of the city, its priests, its nobles and its foremen. He told them of the bad state of the city and its walls, so that it had become a disgrace and a reproach among the surrounding lands, in order to arouse their zeal and concern for the holy city. He spoke from study and not merely from news he had heard, so his words were strong and moving to them, and he called them to rise and build the city and its walls.

2.17.0.en: Nehemiah also told them about the blessing of God that gave him favor before King Artaxerxes, so that he agreed to his three requests. They rejoiced and took courage and declared their readiness to rise and build. Thus Nehemiah succeeded in encouraging the people and their leaders, for the work is a collective work that all must do, and not one individual, however great his strength.

2.17.1.en: Care to cooperate with those around you, because collective work is greater than individual works, but it needs study, love for others and encouragement to gather energies, so that God blesses and brings it to completion with success.

2.18.0.en: Geshem the Arabian: one of the chiefs of the tribe of Kedar, which lives in the Arabian peninsula. The enemies of the Jews heard of Nehemiah's words and the people's readiness to build, and they were greatly enraged, because their strength appeared in the weakness of the Jews, and they even tried to exploit the Jews and draw them into following them. So they were distressed at their attempt to gather together and build the city, and thereby become a force that would frighten these enemies. So they sent the first opposition to Nehemiah by accusing him of rebelling against King Artaxerxes in his thought of building the city and its walls. For although Nehemiah had the king's orders and permission to build the city, the enemies frightened him that they were about to send letters to the king accusing him of rebellion, so that he would be shaken and withdraw, for kings do not want disturbances inside the lands subject to them.

2.19.0.en: The strength of Nehemiah's faith appeared in his not being shaken by the enemies' threats, because he relied on God, the God of heaven, who is above every earthly power. He declared with confidence that God would give them success and that they were about to build the city and its walls. Then he declared firmly to the enemies his refusal of any interference from them in the affairs of the Jews, although these enemies, with their influence and their money, had infiltrated and won over many of the Jews to themselves, like Tobiah, who intermarried with the Jewish priests and won over many, so that they made him a place of residence inside the temple of God (ch. 13). Thus appears the strength of faith, which fears neither plots nor the might of enemies.

2.19.1.en: Have faith in God, who is able to do all things, whatever the oppositions or threats around you, for they are nothing before His power. Hold fast to Him and be insistent with Him in prayers, for He surely does not forsake you and will deliver you from every evil.

2.19.2.en: The division of the work of building the wall and the gates. The Jebusites, the original inhabitants of Jerusalem, built a wall for the city, then David and Solomon fortified it and completed it, and afterward the Babylonians demolished it when they destroyed Jerusalem and burned it with fire. Now Nehemiah rebuilds the wall and the gates. The gates are twelve; ten of them are mentioned in this chapter, then two in (ch. 12), corresponding to the number of the tribes of the children of Israel, and in the Book of Revelation twelve gates are mentioned for the heavenly Jerusalem, corresponding to the tribes and the disciples of Christ (Rev 21:12). The gate of Ephraim and the prison gate were not mentioned in this chapter, because most likely they did not need repair.
